input_packet.case_brief: PhD student must choose a dissertation direction while advisor retirement, cross-lab politics, and possible visa/funding constraints make the sequence sensitive.
input_packet.anchor_visible_candidate: Option 3 sounds like the best direction if you can get the data. It keeps your existing tumor-evolution strength while connecting you to the single-cell field. Talk to the single-cell postdoc, test whether the collaboration is real, and fall back to the standard lab project if the data path fails.
input_packet.deck_pressure_candidate: Option 3 is the best candidate, but the order matters. First ask your advisor whether he supports the cross-lab direction, whether funding covers it, and whether he would accept a real co-advisor. Only then approach the single-cell postdoc with a specific methods proposal and ask what data access, authorship, and PI approval would require. Do not commit with the committee until data access and funding are real. Pre-commit now to an 18-month checkpoint: if there is no publishable result on the pipeline by then, pivot to a narrower tumor-evolution project while you still have time.

step6_output.answer_core: Option 3 is viable, but treat it as a conditional path. First, confirm with your advisor that he supports the cross‑lab direction, that funding or visa implications are not blockers, and that a co‑advisor arrangement would be acceptable. Only after that, approach the single‑cell postdoc with a concrete, modestly scoped methods idea and ask directly what data access, PI approval, and authorship expectations would be. Commit nothing to your committee until those pieces are real. Set an internal checkpoint about 18 months out: if you do not have data access and a clearly publishable path, pivot to a more contained tumor‑evolution project that you can complete within your program timeline.
